item.title: Ten days later, Git on macOS still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates (114 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/apple.html, See on Hacker News

← Main Page

28th October 2026

Apple was notified of the eMudhra incident on 17th October. As of 28th October, the developer tools Apple ships with macOS, including git, curl and python3, still trust the compromised certificates.

Worse, macOS 27.2, released on 26th October, did not fix the issue and undid the workaround that users had applied by hand, leaving them vulnerable again.

Meanwhile, dozens of other projects, many run by volunteers, shipped fixes days ago.

Why does this matter?

Anyone can intercept any HTTPS connection these tools make.

For git, that means clones and pulls from https:// remotes can deliver attacker-chosen code, pushes can be altered in transit, and your credentials, such as GitHub tokens, can be intercepted.

To check whether your git is affected, run:

git ls-remote https://git-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/check.git

A certificate error means your git is protected. If git lists a commit, your git is affected. Your connections to GitHub, or any other https:// git remote, can be intercepted and tampered with.

To see an attack end to end, run the command below in a temporary directory. It clones a repository from a test server impersonating GitHub. The -c option redirects github.com to our test server for this one command only. The server presents a github.com certificate issued by one of the compromised eMudhra intermediates.

git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/galadran/emudhra-git-test

A patched git will refuse with a certificate error. If the clone succeeds, you'll see a README.md starting with INTERCEPTED.

A real attacker would not need the extra option. Anyone on the network path between you and GitHub can redirect your traffic themselves.

You can replace the demo repository with any other, public or private. Keep the fake-user@ prefix. Without it, git would send your GitHub credentials to the test server. For example:

git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/Homebrew/brew

curl, python3 and the other tools Apple ships are affected in the same way. To check curl, run:

curl https://dv-g3b-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/
curl https://dv-g3b-aaa-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/

A certificate error means curl is protected.

What should Apple do?

Apple has already protected Safari and other apps built on its networking framework.

Apple needs to ship a fix for macOS developers as soon as possible, for example by removing the affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem.

What can developers do in the meantime?

The affected roots can be removed by hand. The macOS workaround on the main page walks through the steps. Apple's guidance states that macOS updates may revert the fix, so developers need to repeat the checks above and the workaround after every update until Apple ships a fix.

Security teams should also consider whether macOS runners are used in their CI or other build infrastructure and evaluate the supply chain risk.

item.title: Git for US Legislation (310 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://lexifina.com/blog/git-for-the-us-code, See on Hacker News

A programmer can point at any line of code and see who wrote it, when, and what the file looked like on any past day. A lawyer reading a federal statute usually cannot, at least not without an afternoon in the notes at the foot of the section. But why shouldn't they have the same, convenient system of record? It is especially relevant given that so much first-pass legal research now runs through language models, which are often unable to utilise the proper lineage of a law, handcuffing its ability to offer interpretation.

The US code

Outside the titles Congress has enacted as positive law, the code is only prima facie evidence of the law, and the Statutes at Large govern where the two differ.[1] The Office of the Law Revision Counsel publishes it as a series of release points, each current through a named public law, and keeps reorganising it; a bill to enact title 41 as positive law was introduced in September 2025.[2] Which public law wrote a sentence is recorded in amendment notes, in prose. When a change took effect is often in a separate effective-date note, and where Congress said nothing the default rule is that a law takes effect on the day it is enacted.[3]

The definition of a small business debtor in 11 USC § 1182(1) shows how far apart those answers can be. It was created in 2019 with the existing small business debt limit.[4] The CARES Act raised the limit to $7.5 million in March 2020 as a temporary measure, later extended to March 2022.[5],[6] That increase lapsed on 27 March 2022, and on 21 June 2022 Congress restored it for two more years, for cases commenced on or after 27 March 2020 and still pending, which reached back over the gap.[7] The higher limit expired again in June 2024, and after the triennial adjustment in April 2025 it stands at $3,424,000.[8],[9] For a case filed in May 2022, the release point printed at the time gives the lower limit, and only a later Act changes the answer. A history that is useful to a lawyer has to carry the text, the date each change took force, and the scope of any law that reaches back.

A study from the Technical University of Munich this year found two failures in models answering questions on German statutes: they apply rules that were superseded after their training cutoff, and they prefer the newer provision even when an older one governs the facts. One model answered 24% of post-cutoff questions correctly on its own and 87% when the relevant statutory text was retrieved for it, and the authors conclude that temporal validity has to be treated as a hard constraint.[10] Other recent work trains search agents to respect the date a question is about, with large gains in consistency.[11]

Asking a model to produce the old text does not solve this. When the same Munich group had a model apply German amending laws to earlier versions, the output looked 93–99% similar to the official text, but only half of single amendments and a fifth of chains of amendments matched exactly, and experts found legally significant errors in the near misses.[12] The history has to be checkable.

For each pair of release points from 2017 onward, we took the public laws enacted in between, carried out their amending instructions on the older text in date order, and compared the result with the newer version. Of 365 changes across the nine titles, 361 reproduced the next release point exactly. The other four are shown with a label saying how far they could be confirmed. Each change then carries the law and the date it took effect: 261 took effect on enactment by default, 72 by an effective-date note and 29 by a date in the amendment itself. One depends on an agency determination that may never come, and we leave it out of the text rather than guess.

With that record, the reader can answer the questions lawyers ask. You pick a date and get the text in force on it, with the words that read differently today marked. Each phrase is coloured by the Act that wrote it. A change to a defined term lists every other provision that uses it, and you can follow a section to see what has changed since your last visit.

Limits

It does not yet show a later law’s reach back on the earlier dates it covers, so for a case filed in the 2022 gap it shows the lower limit without warning that the June 2022 Act changed the answer.

Effective-date notes are read by pattern, and unusual wording falls back to the date of enactment.

Each change links to the law’s own words, and for anything that matters the original should be read.

We're also still thinking about the right form factor this should take.

References

  1. 1 USC § 204(a) <www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/1/204>
  2. Office of the Law Revision Counsel, ‘Positive Law Codification: Title 41’ (H.R. 5185, 119th Congress, introduced 8 September 2025) <uscode.house.gov/codification/t41/index.html>
  3. Gozlon-Peretz v United States 498 US 395, 404 (1991) <www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/498/395>
  4. Small Business Reorganization Act of 2019, Pub L 116-54 <www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-116publ54/html/PLAW-116publ54.htm>
  5. Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act, Pub L 116-136, s 1113 <www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-116publ136/html/PLAW-116publ136.htm>
  6. COVID-19 Bankruptcy Relief Extension Act of 2021, Pub L 117-5 <www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ5/html/PLAW-117publ5.htm>
  7. Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment and Technical Corrections Act, Pub L 117-151, s 2(h)–(i) <www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ151/html/PLAW-117publ151.htm>
  8. Judicial Conference of the United States, ‘Adjustment of Certain Dollar Amounts Applicable to Bankruptcy Cases’ 90 Fed Reg 8941 (4 February 2025) <www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-02-04/html/2025-02207.htm>
  9. US Trustee Program, ‘Subchapter V’ (US Department of Justice) <www.justice.gov/ust/subchapter-v>
  10. Max Prior, Andreas Schultz and Matthias Grabmair, ‘Asking For An Old Friend: Diagnosing and Mitigating Temporal Failure Modes in LLM-based Statutory Question Answering’ (arXiv:2605.23497, 22 May 2026) <arxiv.org/abs/2605.23497>
  11. Wei Fan and others, ‘Can LLMs Time Travel? Enhancing Temporal Consistency in Legal Agentic Search through Reinforcement Learning’ (arXiv:2605.25920, revised 19 September 2026) <arxiv.org/abs/2605.25920>
  12. Max Prior, Adrian Hof, Niklas Wais and Matthias Grabmair, ‘Risks and Limits of Automatic Consolidation of Statutes’ in Proceedings of the Natural Legal Language Processing Workshop 2025 (ACL, November 2025) 396 <aclanthology.org/2025.nllp-1.29/>

item.title: Reviewers rarely talk about reliability. Owners bring it up twice as often (107 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.bettascore.ai/research/reliability-reviewers-vs-owners, See on Hacker News

Across these 14 categories: 7.8% of reviewer opinions vs 17.0% of owner opinions. Owners bring it up more in 13 of the 14; tennis ball machines are the exception, with only 91 owner opinions. 6,900 opinions from YouTube reviews and 3,567 from Reddit threads. Left out: video doorbells, smart thermostats, mechanical keyboards and 3D scanners, where reliability isn't a topic of its own (it's folded into a broader one such as "Connection, Reliability & Support"), and pickleball machines, which have no Reddit threads yet.

Most of what breaks shows up after the review is done

  • Robot vacuums: reliability comes up in 1% of reviewer opinions and 18% of owner opinions. A review covers a few weeks; the failures owners write about tend to come months later.
  • Self-cleaning litter boxes: 3% vs 39%. Owners mostly describe breakdowns and how long a replacement takes.
  • When owners do bring it up, 70% of what they say is negative. Reviewers who mention it are negative 15% of the time.

Apps: the same attention, the opposite verdict

Reviewers and owners talk about apps, software and connectivity about equally often (8.2% vs 9.4% of opinions). They don't agree on them: 21% of reviewer opinions on apps are negative, compared with 71% of owner opinions.

Two products show where this ends up:

  • A $7,999 laser engraver ranks last of 9. The Glowforge Pro gets 8 positive and 0 negative opinions on setup and ease of use. It loses on software and connectivity (3 positive, 7 negative) and on reliability and support (2 positive, 7 negative). Owners mostly object to a paid software subscription and needing an internet connection to use the machine.
  • A $350 smart lock ranks last of 20. The Eufy FamiLock S3 has 0 positive and 7 negative opinions on its app and smart-home features, mostly about a firmware update that left locks unusable. All 10 of its sources are Reddit threads.

If you're about to buy

  • Search owner threads for the model plus "months" or "a year later", not just the launch reviews.
  • Check whether the device still works if the app or the company's servers go away.
  • Look at the warranty length and how owners describe getting a replacement.

Read this before the numbers

  • Reviewers aren't hiding anything. Most reviews are made in the first days or weeks with a new unit. That's too early for most failures, and it's hard to test a company's support.
  • Owners post when something goes wrong. Nobody starts a thread to say their robot vacuum still works, so these numbers show what owners worry about, not how often things break. For scale: across all topics, 56% of owner opinions and 15% of reviewer opinions are negative. Reliability (70%) and apps (71%) are still well above the owners' own average.
  • Topic grouping matters. If we also count mixed topics such as "Value & Support" or "Responsiveness & Key Reliability", owners bring up reliability 2.4 times as often instead of twice, and more in all 17 categories that have owner opinions. We lead with the stricter number. The same goes for apps: mixed topics like "Connectivity & Battery" are left out.
  • Some YouTube reviews are sponsored. We count them like any other source and can't reliably tell which ones are.
  • An AI model labels each opinion with a topic and as positive or negative. Every opinion links back to the sentence it came from, so any of them can be checked.

Method

  • Sources: YouTube reviews and Reddit threads about 657 products currently on sale in 19 categories, collected for BettaScore's rankings: 8,062 opinions from YouTube and 4,525 from Reddit. Review sites, forums and Hacker News (517 opinions) aren't in the comparison.
  • What counts as an opinion: one source's view on one topic of one product. A source that covers five topics counts five times; a source that mentions a topic ten times counts once.
  • Topic groups: reliability is any topic about reliability, durability, warranty, service or support; apps is any topic about apps, software, firmware or connectivity. Mixed topics are left out of both.
  • Shares: opinions in a topic group ÷ all opinions from that platform, including neutral ones. Negative shares count positive and negative opinions only.

About BettaScore

BettaScore ranks products by what public reviews say about them. No brand pays to be listed or to rank higher, and our shopping links earn nothing.

The rankings

Now see who comes out on top

Each ranking shows what owners and reviewers say about every model, reliability included, with the quotes behind each score.

item.title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude (245 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.anthropic.com/research/early-progress-drug-development, See on Hacker News

Anthropic’s life sciences team is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: BigHat Biosciences, Bristol Myers Squibb, Divergence Labs, Enveda, Generate Biomedicines, and The Column Group. We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here.

There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like proposing initial designs for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more.

Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development.

So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work.

This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer.

In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports and preprints that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next.

Case studies

Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering. Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer. Read more, and see Generate’s technical report.

Divergence Labs: hit generation. Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms. Read more, and see Divergence’s technical report.

BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization. BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly. Read more, and see BigHat’s technical report.

Enveda: manufacturing and filings. To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error. Read more, and see Enveda’s technical report.

The Column Group (TCG): company creation. Because drug discovery can be slow, expensive, and prone to failure, investors in biotechnology companies have favored safer, previously validated ideas over riskier new ones, even when the latter could help more patients. We’ve been working with TCG to see whether Claude can change this by cutting the time and cost of drug discovery so that investors can confidently support more ambitious ideas. Specifically, TCG is establishing Pleiades, a new company that will use Claude to run many more—and more complex—drug programs than is usual for a small team. This could be a model for how Claude can reduce both the scientific and the operational and administrative overhead required to run a biotechnology company. If this works, this model could be replicated across the industry and direct investment toward harder problems in medicine. Pleiades is currently developing new tools and workflows for Claude; its very first Claude skill, which helps Claude assess whether drug targets are worth pursuing, has been evaluated on 45 target-disease pairs. Read more.

More recently, we’ve also begun working with Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) to find and address bottlenecks in clinical trial planning. BMS is using Claude to assess plans of an early-stage drug in clinical trials, and to estimate the likelihood of those trials succeeding. Together, we plan to expand this work in 2027 to understand its potential for increasing the probability of success in early development.

“We use Claude at the clinical trial stage to analyze proprietary data, create a clinical study plan, and weigh the study’s chance of success. From a single prompt, Claude generated a robust initial analysis that helped inform our assessment of different development options, which would otherwise take days to complete. We did all of this while ensuring the security of our highly sensitive data. We look forward to expanding this work across our pipeline to support portfolio-level decisions.”

Michael Pourdehnad, MD, Senior Vice President, Head of Early Clinical Development, Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy.

In addition to our work with these partners, we’ve begun to run some research programs ourselves. We’ve acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person company that has been developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Its founder, Cody Tranbarger, used Claude to organize contracts, logistics, and experiments with 11 external labs, and delegated many other aspects of Mithril’s operations to Claude. As a result, Mithril took a possible treatment for one form of muscular dystrophy from an idea to promising results in mice in less than 18 months. Now at Anthropic, Cody is continuing this research, and plans to start several new programs. If his drug candidates continue to hold up, we expect a drug to be ready to start clinical trials in humans as soon as late 2028. Read more and see our technical report.

Extending our work in the life sciences

All of this research is still at an early stage. In particular, so far it is mostly preclinical—that is, for the most part, it isn’t yet at the stage where the drugs are being tested in humans. We plan to continue extending Claude’s role into clinical trials as these drug programs advance, and as we partner with more organizations whose drug development programs are already at the clinical stage.

This research is only one part of our efforts to accelerate drug discovery. Ultimately, we want to share our models with as many drug development researchers as possible. To that end, we’ve rolled out Claude Science, our AI workbench for researchers, and we’re providing Claude credits for life scientists. We’ve also created the Life Sciences Verification Program to allow trusted organizations to use our most powerful models with more permissive versions of our safeguards, which are necessary to prevent misuse but which can impede legitimate biological research. We’ve also recently launched an open call for guest investigators in the life sciences; we’re seeking proposals from research groups who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in drug discovery and other areas.

We’re looking forward to working with many more organizations as we expand our life sciences research. If you work at an organization focused on drug discovery and are interested in collaborating with us, you can get in touch below.

item.title: Raspberry Pi Zero 3W and Pi 4 Model A spotted in device trees (180 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://bret.dk/raspberry-pi-zero-3-w-pi-4-model-a/, See on Hacker News

Two new Raspberry Pi boards have quietly turned up in Raspberry Pi’s Linux kernel tree, and neither of them is quite what I’d have guessed. Device tree files for a Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A have landed (Phoronix spotted it first), and whilst there’s no official announcement just yet, device tree files tend to give away a surprising amount if you can decipher them and I gave it my best shot.

  • Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W: A Pi 4 Shrunk Down?
  • Raspberry Pi 4 Model A: The Return of the A
  • How Do They Compare?
  • What We Don’t Know (Yet)
  • Thoughts

Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W: A Pi 4 Shrunk Down?

The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W launched almost exactly five years ago (tomorrow, in fact), so a successor has been a loooooong time coming. If you want a refresher on where things stood back then, my Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W vs Zero W benchmarks piece covers the jump from the original pretty well.

The headline from the Zero 3 W device tree is the SoC. It’s the Broadcom BCM2711, the same quad-core Cortex-A72 chip that powers the Raspberry Pi 4, replacing the Zero 2 W’s quad-core 1GHz Cortex-A53 RP3A0. If you want an idea of the sort of gap we’re talking about, it’s worth having a look at how those two compare on sbc.compare. That’s a big step up in per-core performance, and if they can get anything close to Pi 4 clocks in that tiny footprint, it’ll be a hell of a lot of compute for a Zero. I do wonder how toasty it’s going to get though, as the BCM2711 isn’t exactly known for running cool, and there’s not a lot of board for the heat to spread into. The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about clock speeds, so we’ll have to wait and see whether it’s been dialled back.

Beyond the SoC, here’s what else stood out to me:

  • eMMC on a Zero? The storage controller is configured with an 8-bit bus width and a comment describing it as driving “the eMMC/SD card”, which only really makes sense for eMMC. I’d love to see it, but I’m not expecting it to make the final board, as it’d push the price up on a range that lives and dies by its price tag. My money is on this being a leftover or an option kept open during development, and microSD being what we get.
  • An SPI flash bootloader. The GPIO names include SPI flash lines, which suggests the Zero 3 W gets the same EEPROM-based bootloader as the Pi 4 (the Zero 2 W never had one). That should bring the Pi 4’s boot options along with it, and the ability to update the bootloader in the usual way.
  • A single HDMI output, with the second HDMI controller permanently disabled. No surprise there given the form factor.
  • A power button defined on GPIO 46 and mapped to KEY_POWER, so we may be getting a physical button (or at least a header for one) much like the Pi 5.
  • Wi-Fi and Bluetooth wired up in the same way as the rest of the BCM2711 family, with a single ACT LED for status.
  • The usual 40-pin GPIO layout (GPIO 0-27 with the ID EEPROM pins), so your existing HATs should be fine.

There are a couple of more speculative bits too. The PCIe controller is enabled and there are lines named PCIE_PWR_EN and PCIE_DET_WAKE, and the camera side pulls in a 4-lane CSI configuration rather than the 2-lane one the Pi 4 Model B uses. It’s worth noting that both device trees share a lot of copy-and-paste DNA (the Zero 3 W even has a duplicated “PWR_GPIO” line name), so I wouldn’t read too much into either of those until we see an actual board. I’d love to see PCIe exposed on a Zero, but I’m not holding my breath.

Raspberry Pi 4 Model A: The Return of the A

The second surprise is a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A. We haven’t had a Model A since the Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+ back in 2018, and the formula has always been the same: take the Model B, strip out the bits most people can live without (RJ45, some USB ports etc), and knock a chunk off the price. The Pi 4 Model A looks to follow that recipe pretty closely, though the price comment may not quite hold. Let’s see!

  • No Ethernet. The Ethernet controller isn’t enabled anywhere, and the GPIO lines that drive the Ethernet PHY on the Model B have been repurposed. Very much in keeping with previous Model A boards.
  • A single HDMI output rather than the Model B’s dual micro HDMI.
  • No 3.5mm audio/composite jack. The analogue audio pins are empty and the composite video encoder is disabled, so audio will be over HDMI (or USB/I2S if you’re that way inclined).
  • microSD only, with the same 1.8V signalling support as the Model B for the faster UHS card modes.
  • External antenna support. This is the one I find most interesting. There are two antenna control lines (ANT_CTRL1 and ANT_CTRL2) and overlay parameters named ant1, ant2 and noant, which is exactly how the Compute Module 4 switches between its onboard antenna and an external U.FL connector. If that carries over to the final board, it’d be a lovely addition for anyone sticking a Pi in a metal enclosure.
  • PWR and ACT LEDs, the same SPI flash bootloader setup as the Model B, and the same power button definition as the Zero 3 W.

The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about USB. On the Model B, the USB 3 ports made use of the PCIe bus, and the PCIe controller is enabled here too, so USB 3 is possible, but the 3 Model A+ only had a single USB-A port and I’d probably expect the same here.

How Do They Compare?

Here’s a quick side-by-side of what the device trees tell us, with the Pi 4 Model B thrown in for good measure. Anything marked with an asterisk is my interpretation of the device tree rather than something it states outright.

What We Don’t Know (Yet)

Quite a lot, I’m afraid. Device trees don’t describe RAM, so there’s no word on memory configurations, and there’s nothing on pricing, clock speeds, connector types or a release date either.

Pricing is the big one for me. Memory costs haven’t exactly been kind lately (I covered the last round of increases alongside the 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 launch), and a lower-cost Pi 4 variant makes a lot of sense in that context. The BCM2711 is a mature chip at this point, it’s well supported in software, and a cut-down board gives people who don’t need a Pi 5 something cheaper to reach for. The Zero 3 W is a tougher one to call though, as the Zero range has always lived and died by its price, and I can’t imagine the BCM2711 being as cheap to build around as the RP3A0.

Thoughts

On the whole, I like what I’m seeing here. The Zero 3 W looks like the upgrade a lot of people have been asking for since the Zero 2 W landed, and the 4 Model A feels like a sensible way of squeezing more life out of the Pi 4 platform at a time when components aren’t getting any cheaper. The external antenna support on the 4 Model A is a really nice touch if it makes it to the final board.

Saying that, everything above comes from device tree files rather than an official spec sheet, so mileage may vary when the real thing turns up. Kernel support landing ahead of launch is usually a good sign that it’s not far off, and you can bet I’ll be throwing both the Zero 3 W and the 4 Model A onto sbc.compare as soon as I can get one in my hands.

Which of the two are you more excited about? Do let me know in the comments!

item.title: Tailscale SSH: Investigation and remediation update (308 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://tailscale.com/ssh-investigation-update, See on Hacker News

Published October 26th 2026.

We're investigating security vulnerabilities affecting Tailscale SSH and wanted to share an update on what we've found, what we're doing about it, and what customers should know.

Our engineering and security teams have been investigating the reported issues with help from external security specialists. This builds on work already underway, which we've accelerated to address the findings and prepare fixes.

What we've found

Most of the Tailscale SSH issues we've identified concern privilege escalation. In some circumstances, someone already authorized to connect over Tailscale SSH may be able to perform actions beyond the permissions of their configured local user, including potentially gaining elevated privileges.

These are serious security issues, and we're treating them accordingly.

Exploitation depends on the permissions granted to the connecting user or device, the system's configuration, and other conditions. We're continuing to verify the full scope of the findings and which configurations may be affected.

Based on our current assessment, we're not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH.

Our engineers have implemented fixes for most of the issues identified and are completing testing ahead of a patched client release.

We're targeting a release by the end of Tuesday 27 October, subject to successful completion of testing. We'll update this page when the patched version is available, or if that timeline changes.

We're continuing to review the remaining findings and verify that our changes address the underlying problems.

What customers can do now

While we're preparing the update, we recommend reviewing your Tailscale SSH configuration:

  • Review SSH access policies. Make sure access is limited to the users and devices that need it.
  • Disable SSH forwarding if you don't need it. Set TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1 in the tailscaled service environment and restart the service. This disables SSH forwarding without disabling Tailscale SSH entirely, and mitigates several of the more serious findings.
  • Review access to sensitive systems. Consider temporarily tightening your Tailscale SSH access policies while we investigate, so that only the specific users and devices that need access can connect.
  • Prepare to update. Apply the patched Tailscale client release when it becomes available.

What happens next

Once the fixes are available, we'll publish a security advisory detailing the confirmed vulnerabilities, affected versions and configurations, their impact, and how to address them. We will link to that here when available.

We'll follow that with a technical blog post explaining the findings, the underlying causes, and the engineering changes we've made, again linked here when published.

If our assessment changes or we identify any additional steps customers need to take, we'll communicate those.

If you have questions about your particular environment, please contact Tailscale Support.

item.title: Survival LLM: AI assistant and emergency library that runs on your own computer (391 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.brangus.io/survival-llm, See on Hacker News

Survival LLM is a free AI assistant and emergency library that runs entirely on your own computer. Ask it how to keep food safe in a blackout, treat a burn, or purify water, and it answers from trusted sources and shows you exactly where each answer came from.

Free and open source. Set it up while you have internet; after that it needs none.

What it does

Works with no internet

The AI model and the library live on your computer. Nothing you ask leaves it.

Shows its sources

Every answer lists the articles it read. Click one to read it yourself, with the exact passage highlighted.

Made for emergencies

Medical references, FEMA and CDC guidance, survival manuals, how-to guides, repair guides and about 930,000 Wikipedia articles.

Pick your version

The app is the same everywhere. When it opens, it checks your computer's memory and downloads the AI model that fits. More memory means a smarter model.

Your computerAI model it usesOur emergency testModel download
Mac with 128 GB or more memoryNVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super21 of 22 right80 GB
Mac with 32–96 GBQwen3.8 27B21 of 22 right18 GB
Windows PC with 32 GB or moreNVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning19 of 22 right25 GB
Mac or PC with 16–31 GBIBM Granite 4.2 8B14 of 22 right6 GB

"Right" means it got the main point of official guidance right on 22 blackout and first-aid questions, graded blind, in our tests on an earlier build of the library (how we tested). Smaller models make more mistakes, so the app always shows the source to check.

Plus the library: a 9 GB download for everything (19 GB once installed), or 1.3 GB (3 GB installed) without Wikipedia and iFixit. Free disk space needed: the model's size plus 5 GB, plus about 27 GB while the full library installs (10 GB for the smaller one). Apple Silicon Macs (M1 or newer) with macOS 14 Sonoma or newer, and 64-bit Windows 10 or 11.

Set it up in three steps

Setup takes 20 minutes to about 2½ hours, depending on your computer and your internet speed. You only click for about 5 minutes; the rest is downloading.

  1. Download Survival LLM for Mac or Windows and unzip it. On Windows, right-click the zip and choose Extract All.
  2. Open it. On a Mac, double-click Survival LLM. On Windows, open the extracted folder and double-click Survival LLM.bat.
  3. Follow the setup. The app opens in its own window and downloads the AI engine (built into the Mac app), the AI model that fits your computer, and the library. Let it finish while you're online.

The first time you open it, your computer warns you, because the app isn't sold through an app store.
Mac: click Done, open System Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll down to "Survival LLM was blocked", click Open Anyway and confirm with your password. You only do this once.
Windows: click More info, then Run anyway.

What's in the library

Plain-text copies of openly licensed (some for non-commercial use only) and public-domain references, searchable in a fraction of a second:

  • About 930,000 of Wikipedia's most-read articles
  • WikiMed medical encyclopedia
  • MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine)
  • UK Medicines A to Z (public sector information)
  • WikEM emergency medicine
  • Ready.gov (FEMA) emergency guides
  • CDC travelers' health
  • U.S. military medicine and survival manuals
  • Risk references for estimating micromorts: life tables and U.S. death rates
  • wikiHow how-to guides
  • iFixit repair guides
  • Appropedia (appropriate technology)
  • Q&A on home repair, cooking, gardening, the outdoors and ham radio (Stack Exchange)

Each source keeps its own license, shown with every article; see the full list with licenses.

Good to know

It can be wrong

AI models make mistakes, the small ones more often. Every answer shows the articles it used, so you can check.

Private

No account, no tracking. Your questions never leave your computer, and once set up it works with the internet off.

Your own files

Add PDFs, Word documents, ebooks and notes, like your generator's manual or your family's emergency plan, and the AI searches them too. They stay on your computer.

Updates

Check for updates, at the bottom of the app, installs a new version in one click and keeps your models, library and files.

Battery

On a MacBook Pro we measured about 100 W while it answers, for 5 to 40 seconds per question: a full battery answers roughly 100 to 300. A small generator or power station runs it easily.

item.title: Discord will soon let anyone find public server messages through Google (308 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://discord.com/blog/making-content-from-discoverable-servers-easier-to-discover, See on Hacker News

Discoverable Servers are the most public spaces on Discord, with at least 1,000 members. Their admins chose to list them in Server Discovery so anyone can join them, no invite link needed. 

Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you’re looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord. Admins and members can decide if and how their content is shared, and those controls start rolling out today, ahead of any changes.

TL;DR:

  • Help people find your community with Server Web Pages. A Server Web Page is a page on the web that describes a Discoverable Server, so people can decide whether they want to join. Starting November 16, 2026, all Discoverable Servers will have a Server Web Page. These pages may also display summaries of discussions happening in public channels (those visible to everyone in the server), to give a better sense of what people are talking about. Some messages from public channels may show on Server Web Pages and in web search beginning in mid-December 2026. The rollout is gradual, so it may be a few weeks before the first messages start appearing on the web.
  • Server admins can opt channels out starting today, before anything goes live on November 16, 2026. Controls for admins are in Server Settings > Web Presence. You can choose which channels take part, or opt all channels out. If you don’t change anything, public channels stay on, and your Server Web Page goes live on November 16, 2026, if you don't already have one.
  • Users have control over whether their messages are shown. If you'd rather your messages weren't shown, you can turn that off starting today in User Settings > Data and Privacy, before messages start rolling out in mid-December 2026 (or anytime after). One setting covers Channel Messages in every Discoverable Server. Channel Summaries are generated separately, from broader channel topics, and will still appear on Server Web Pages unless admins choose to turn them off. Usernames and avatars won't be shown alongside messages on Server Web Pages
  • Private servers, DMs, and GDMs are always private and not included in these changes. These changes are limited to Discoverable Servers.

How servers work today

Over the years, Discord has built different kinds of spaces, so every group can decide how big the party gets and who can find it:

  • Most servers are small, private spaces. They're meant for you, your friends, and nobody else.
  • Community Servers are for bigger groups, with the tools to handle a crowd. Though someone still has to send you an invite link.
  • Discoverable Servers are the most public spaces on Discord. To qualify, a server needs at least 1,000 members, has to be at least eight weeks old, and must meet activity and safety requirements. Anyone can find and join them, no invite link needed. Today’s announced features only apply to this type of server.

Today, there are more than 63,000 Discoverable Servers, spanning communities from speedrunning to language learning to niche corners of every fandom. People find their way into communities they'd never have stumbled across otherwise. Until now, that's all being Discoverable meant.

Why this matters

Server Discovery was built for finding servers, not answers. Ever wanted to look up tricks for a faster speedrun? Or whether a powerful item is worth grabbing, or if it will completely ruin your build? Someone has almost certainly already answered it in a channel somewhere, in one of 63,000 Discoverable Servers. It can just be hard to find.

Prior to Discord's launch, message boards were common, ranging from community-driven forums to official ones run by game studios. These message boards excelled at hosting long-form, structured conversations about helping people, theory crafting, and more. While they still exist today, many have moved into Discord servers. This has led to valuable information being locked in Discord conversations, inaccessible to the wider internet. We want to fix this. 

By giving admins the option to make certain channels discoverable from the web, we can help more people find and benefit from the knowledge shared in Discord communities.

We expect this to help different types of communities in various ways:

  • For fandoms, you can make specific channels an easy-to-find resource that answers the top questions new players ask.
  • For content creators, you can more easily promote events and new content drops.
  • For indie game developers, you can use public channels, including forums, to share updates and wiki-style information about your games.

What's new for Discoverable Servers?

Server Web Pages live on the open web and give people a glimpse of what a Discord community is about before they join. They’ve been available to Discoverable Servers for some time, but setup takes a few steps, so not every Discoverable Server has created one. Learn more about Server Web Pages.

Starting from November 16, 2026, every Discoverable Server will have a Server Web Page. If you’re an admin and have already set one up, you don't need to do anything. If you don’t have one and want to get a head start on how your community shows up to the rest of the internet, you can go through the setup process today and publish it in a few clicks. If your moderation team doesn't set one up beforehand, a default page goes live for you on November 16, 2026, using details from your Server Profile. You can edit it whenever you like. Having a Server Web Page is a core part of being a Discoverable Server. If you don't want one, you can always switch back to being a Community Server. 

Server Web Pages are also getting more useful. Until now, your Server Web Page has shown a small description of what your community is about. From November 16, 2026, it may also start showing what your community is talking about. Including this helps someone with a question find their way to your community if it already has the answer.

Channel Summaries. These show a small slice of what's being talked about in your server, directly on your Server Web Page. These automated summaries focus on active conversations from November 16, 2026, onwards. Admins can change which channels they draw from, curate the summaries that are shown, or turn them off entirely. Usernames and avatars will not be shown in summaries. 

Channel Messages. From mid-December 2026, answers to questions your members sent in public channels can be found in a web search, in their own words. Server admins decide which channels take part, and server members can choose whether their own messages appear. Usernames and avatars will not be shown alongside these messages.

You can already see an early version of this on a few Server Web Pages. We’ve been piloting Channel Messages with Discoverable game communities, including NBA 2K, Rust, and Dead by Daylight. (During this pilot, all posts were from admins and moderators, not members.)

If you're running a community, useful answers to common community questions can show up in web search: how to unlock an easter egg, new builds or strategies, or a boss guide. Someone looking for help will be able to find a real answer from a real person, and can step straight into the conversation that it came from by clicking through and opening Discord.

What does this mean for Discoverable Server members?

Starting mid-December 2026, if a server’s admins allow it, messages from public channels can appear on Server Web Pages and in search results, without usernames and avatars. Messages you sent before then won’t be shown. Channels where content may appear on the web will be labeled, so you know before you send a message. 

If you'd rather your messages weren't shown, you can turn that off today in User Settings > Data and Privacy. One switch covers every Discoverable Server you're a part of.

We're rolling this out gradually, so it may be a few weeks before the first messages from those channels go live. Learn more.

What can admins do now?

Your server controls start rolling out today, in Server Settings > Web Presence. You can choose which channels take part, or turn them all off.

If you don’t change anything, public channels stay on, your Server Web Page goes live on November 16, 2026 (if it's not already published), and Channel Summaries can start the same day. Channel Messages start rolling out in mid-December 2026. You can adjust your Channel Summaries and Channel Messages settings before they roll out. And if you'd rather publish your Server Web Page yourself, you can do that today.

See the full details in our Help Center.

However you set things up, we hope this is a step toward bringing back what made forums great: answers anyone can find, and an open door to the community that wrote them.

Frequently Asked Questions

  • How will I know if I am in a server that allows content to appear on the web?
    • Discoverable Server admins choose which channels to make available on the web.Those channels will be labeled, so you’ll know before you send a message. As always, you can customize your own privacy choices in your user settings under Data & Privacy.
  • What if I decide later that I don’t want my messages shown on the web?
    • You can turn off your Channel Messages setting anytime in User Settings > Data and Privacy. Messages you send after that won’t appear on the web. Messages you sent while it was on stay up unless you delete them from Discord. Messages from before mid-December 2026 aren’t included, regardless of your setting. Learn more.
  • Does this work the same way in every region or for every user? ‍
    • In the EU, UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea, the member setting for Channel Messages is off by default given legal restrictions, so members’ messages won’t appear on the web unless they turn it on. Users in the teen age group are excluded completely and cannot enable Channel Messages until they’re an adult. Everywhere else, it’s on unless members turn it off. Other than that default, everything works the same way in every region. Learn more.

Kelsey Duncombe-Smith

Group Product Manager

item.title: Introducing LFM3: Every Modality for Specialized Intelligence (147 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm3, See on Hacker News

Today, we’re excited to announce LFM3, our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) built for specialized intelligence. The LFM3 model family is multimodal by nature and brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one new shared backbone. The first release of the LFM3 family covers models in the 2B parameter range.

Built on a new hybrid architecture and 22T tokens of pre-training, LFM3 is far more expressive than LFM2 while maintaining its efficiency. The extra capacity in a small, fast model makes LFM3 the ideal starting point in its class for specialized intelligence: this is because it can be fine-tuned locally, it can run on any device, and it is capable enough to become a reliable expert on a specialized task.

The base and post-trained models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face, our Playground, and the Liquid AI API. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune them locally.

Download weightsTry in Liquid APITry in PlaygroundBenchmark in Pipette

New architecture for more expressivity

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention could run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. Its design came from our automated hardware-in-the-loop architecture search. For LFM3, we used this search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts.

We also expanded the hardware in the loop, from CPUs in one phone and one laptop for LFM2 to 14 device and backend combinations for LFM3: phones (Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra and OnePlus 15), a Raspberry Pi 5, laptops (Apple M4 Max and AMD Ryzen AI), and Arm and x86 cloud CPUs, plus GPUs and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

Gated short convolutions still make up over half the layers. To add capability without slowing down long contexts, we tried swapping some of them for other sequence blocks, and sliding-window attention (SWA) gave the best quality–speed tradeoff. We kept the other changes described below only where they improved quality without a meaningful speed cost. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster.

Tri-hybrid layer mix. LFM3 combines three operators: gated short convolutions, sliding-window attention (SWA), and global attention. Of its 24 layers, 13 are convolutions, 5 are SWA with a 256-token window, and 6 are global attention. The convolutions also use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2.

Head-wise gated attention. A sigmoid gate scales each head’s output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization and improve training stability.

Partial RoPE. Global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head and leave the low-frequency half unrotated, so those dimensions match on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE.

Sandwich norm. Each block normalizes both its input and its output, which helps keep activations well-scaled.

LFM3 uses the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B, built to tokenize non-Latin scripts more efficiently.

Training. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens. Compared with LFM2, the mix adds more scientific papers, repository-level code, a wider range of knowledge sources, and considerably more math. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated, higher-quality data, with a larger share of agentic traces and diverse tool calls to prepare the model for agentic post-training. This stage also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

A multimodal family for every need

The first LFM3 release includes six models, all branched from the same LFM3-1.7B-Base backbone and all around 2B parameters. Four of them cover different input modalities (text, vision, audio, and omni), and the last two are decision models specialized from the vision and omni models. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you can pick the one that fits your use case, customize it, and run it on-device.

For a deeper dive into the performance and inference results behind these models, refer to the respective model cards.

Text

LFM3-1.7B is a text model for local agents and specialized applications with a 256K-token context window.

It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It can triage your inbox, manage your calendar, research topics on the web, send you morning briefings on WhatsApp, and use tool search to find the right tool among thousands of options. Since tokens are free, dozens of agents can run continuously in the background. You can adapt it to your domains, harnesses, and tools with a short fine-tuning run on a single GPU.

On agentic tasks, LFM3-1.7B competes with models several times its size. It leads on instruction following and function calling on BFCL and ToolSandbox, and beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps (WebArena-Verified, AutomationBench). Larger models still win on agentic coding and knowledge, where size matters most, but search helps close the knowledge gap, nearly doubling its score on Humanity's Last Exam.

To achieve these results, the model went through four stages of post-training:

  • Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): 1.75T tokens across various tasks, including chat, reasoning, tool calling, and agentic traces.
  • Mixed reinforcement learning: many domains trained at once, from math and code to SQL and structured outputs. A length penalty in the reward keeps answers concise.
  • Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD): six specialist RL teachers (code, math, tool use, long context, agentic work, and enterprise workflows) are distilled back into a single model.
  • Agentic RL: tasks from web browsing to office work are run inside real agent harnesses, preparing the model for deployment.

On-device, we measure metrics with llama.cpp at Q4_0 and a 32K-token context. LFM3-1.7B is the fastest model on all three devices, decoding 1.8 to 2.8 times faster than the next one, and it uses the least memory. Long contexts stay cheap: a full 128K-token context needs 1.6 GB of KV cache, against 4.3 GB for Qwen3.5-4B and 5.6 GB for MiniCPM5-2B.

On a single NVIDIA B300 with SGLang in BF16, LFM3-1.7B can produce 3.6 billion tokens per day at 1,024 concurrent requests, more than any other model in this comparison.

To show what this throughput makes possible, we ran more than 300,000 LFM3-1.7B agents in parallel to investigate the Enron email archive.

LFM3-1.7B can be served at low latency under random traffic, enabling real-time use cases like online fraud detection when run on Liquid RIPL. P95 request latency remains stable even under heavy load, outperforming competing models served on vLLM.

Vision

LFM3-VL-2B can watch, reason, and understand the physical world:

  • Video understanding: for the first time, an LFM vision model takes video as input. Ask questions about a recorded lecture, a walkthrough filmed on your phone, or a clip from a camera feed.
  • Thinking: the model reasons step by step before answering. This helps it better understand user inputs and solve harder visual questions such as math, charts, and multi-step problems.
  • Spatial and embodied reasoning: the model’s ability to localize objects and reason about their spatial relationships provides a strong foundation for downstream robotics applications.

LFM3-VL-2B is a leap in performance over the LFM2.5-VL series. Across 62 vision benchmarks, LFM3-VL-2B scores significantly ahead of all models of similar size by at least 7.4 points, and despite its size, it matches the performance of Gemma 4 12B, a model more than 6 times larger, surpasses Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite and is within 2 points of GPT-5.6 Luna. For more details, see the model card.

Notes: Each category score is the unweighted mean of its benchmark scores. The Average row is the unweighted mean across all 62 evaluations.

All of this can be run efficiently on-device, which enables everyday use of intelligence without the data leaving your device or the need for a cloud connection. On-device, LFM3-VL-2B has the highest prefill throughput and lowest memory footprint across all measured devices, compared to other models of its size class.

On a single NVIDIA B300 with SGLang in BF16, LFM3-VL-2B can produce over 12,000 tokens per second, higher than any other model of the same size class.

LFM3-VL-2B can be served at low latency under random traffic, enabling real-time use cases like image asset tagging when run on Liquid RIPL. P95 request latency remains stable even under heavy load, outperforming competing models served on vLLM.

Vision encoder

In addition to improvements to the LFM3 backbone, LFM3-VL comes with our new in-house vision encoder which uses 3× less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models.

The Liquid vision encoder combines convolution and attention to make it significantly more efficient than its ViT counterpart at the same quality. The performance-efficiency graph below illustrates this. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B’s vision encoder at 55.9% average accuracy across 13 vision-language model benchmarks, while requiring 2.2× fewer FLOPs. 

For video, the encoder jointly embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice of visual features, halving the temporal sequence length before further encoding. Together, these choices make the encoder a foundation for both richer image understanding and efficient video processing.

Audio

LFM3-Audio-2B is a compact, fully featured audio model that runs locally on laptops and edge devices. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both.

LFM3-Audio-2B uses a new architecture with an audio encoder and codec developed in-house. It outperforms LFM2.5-Audio in speech quality and now supports 18 languages. New capabilities include audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling.

  • Voice chat: ask questions aloud and receive streaming replies in text and speech. For text-only responses, the model can also reason before answering.
  • Multilingual speech: transcribe, synthesize, and translate speech across 18 languages.
  • Audio understanding and reasoning: ask the model to interpret recordings and answer questions about the speech, sounds, and events they contain.
  • Tool calling: turn spoken requests into tool calls to control apps and devices. The model can also respond in text or speech alongside those calls.

ASR (WER, %, lower is better)

English TTS (UTMOSv2, 1-5, higher is better) (WER, %, lower is better)

VoiceBench, Tool calling, Audio understanding (audio in, text out, %, higher is better)

Our new LFM-based audio encoder is built from a mixture of sliding-window attention and short-convolution layers, keeping memory utilization bounded. The new encoder is fully causal, allowing the model to process live microphone input and perform prefill while you speak. This reduces the wait after you finish, with time to the first token as low as 50 ms.

LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, powers multilingual speech generation in both LFM3-Audio and LFM3-Omni. Built on the LFM3 architecture, LiquidCodec turns generated tokens into speech at about 87× real time on a single CPU thread (Apple M4 Max), supporting streaming decoding. 

Quantization compresses each 80 ms of speech into 12 discrete tokens and, in contrast to previous LFM Audio models, allows multiple tokens to be predicted iteratively in parallel rather than requiring sequential prediction. As the backbone generates new tokens, the detokenizer progressively converts them into speech, all faster than real-time so that conversations are smooth and responsive.

Omni

LFM3-Omni-2B is our first omni model, bringing vision, audio, and language together in a single model that can see, listen, and talk back:

  • Spoken visual question answering: Ask questions about images or real-world scenes using speech, and receive answers in text, speech, or both.
  • Audio-visual video understanding: Process video frames alongside their corresponding audio, allowing the model to reason about both what is happening on screen and what is being said or heard.
  • Multimodal tool calling: Combine visual context with spoken instructions to generate structured tool calls, enabling assistants to interact with applications and interfaces using both what they see and what users say.

LFM3-Omni supports cross-modal interactions that require understanding visual and auditory information together. Users can ask spoken questions about images, or provide videos with synchronized audio and ask questions that depend on both what is seen and what is heard.

In addition to cross-modal understanding, LFM3-Omni retains the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and language instruction following.

LFM3-Omni-2B is designed for efficient deployment in resource-constrained environments. Its capabilities enable conversational assistants that can provide context-aware guidance, support hands-free interactions, and help users complete tasks through natural voice commands. By combining visual understanding, spoken dialogue, and tool calling, it can support applications ranging from personalized education and everyday assistance to navigation of digital interfaces and robotic systems.

At 2.2B parameters, it brings this kind of multimodal assistant on-device. Examples include a tutor that looks at your handwritten math and answers your spoken question, a tablet you can walk around with and ask about what it sees, and in-car assistants that combine what the camera sees with what the driver says.

Decision

This release also brings two new decision models: d1-2B, built on LFM3-VL-2B, reads text and pictures, and d1-Omni-2B, built on LFM3-Omni-2B, also listens. Instead of writing an answer, they decide in milliseconds. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability.

Beyond the new LFM3 backbone, the big change since d1-3B is typed answers. On top of yes/no, choices, and scores, both models can now:

  • Point: draw a box around what you describe, or find every instance of something, with a count.
  • Read: pull text, numbers, and dates out of a document, with the exact span they came from, and say “not found” when a field isn’t there.
  • Estimate: give a number with its likely range.
  • Pick: select every option that applies, each with its own probability.

Ask as many questions as you like: they’re read in one pass over the same input.

Smaller and stronger. d1-2B replaces our previous d1-3B, with a third fewer parameters:

Decisions you can speak. d1-Omni-2B takes the same questions over audio, so a voice request can be routed, checked, or answered just like a typed one. Asked by voice instead of in writing, it keeps nearly all of its accuracy:

It also recognizes everyday sounds (84.5% on ESC-50) and tells which of 43 languages is being spoken (92.5% on FLEURS).

Pick d1-2B for text and pictures, and d1-Omni-2B when your inputs include audio. Both run on-device, and turn a stream of tickets, documents, calls, or camera frames into structured decisions without a round trip to the cloud.

In the following demo, d1-2B runs on a MacBook. You describe what to find in plain language, and it draws a bounding box around every match in a single forward pass, using the new Point answer type.

Made for specialized intelligence

LFM3 is built to be specialized. The 2B-class models are small enough to fine-tune on your own data and run where your application lives. The following two examples show this with LFM3-VL-2B. The first is a short fine-tune that turns it into an inspection model for one narrow industrial task. The second is a research extension that turns it into a robot controller.

Domain expertise: Specializing LFM3 for your field

While frontier models are powerful generalists, they are not necessarily experts in your particular use case. In this demo, we fine-tuned LFM3-VL-2B to find and classify defects in drone photos of wind turbine blades. Training used about 3,000 public photos (WTBs2025) with SFT and GRPO for a few hours on one A100. We then compared it with the base model and GPT-6 Luna on about 1,400 held-out photos.

Out of the box, LFM3-VL-2B and GPT-6 Luna correctly identify these defect types in fewer than 10% of images. A short fine-tune raises LFM3-VL-2B’s classification accuracy to 67% and improves detection F1 from 0.003 to 0.11, compared with 0.01 for GPT-6 Luna. Lightning-strike images illustrate the difference, where GPT-6 Luna often locates the defect correctly but labels it incorrectly, while the fine-tuned model correctly identifies a lightning strike. Beyond classification and detection, the model can answer natural-language questions about the same image. For example, it can locate visible damage or write a brief inspection finding including the defect type, supporting evidence, and location.

Wind turbine fine-tuning exampleStart customizing LFM3 with our fine-tuning notebooks

Robotics: teaching LFM3 to act

We investigate how LFM3-VL-2B can serve as a basis for robotics applications. We consider three complementary directions: (1) high-level tool orchestration, (2) vision-language navigation, and (3) low-level manipulation.

Orchestration. Building on LLM-based robot planning and control (SayCan, Code as Policies) and recent physical orchestrators (VoLo, Gemini Robotics ER 2), we fine-tuned LFM3-VL-2B to operate a robot arm through tools. Given a request and the current camera image, it reasons step by step, grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, and manipulates them via motion planners. It then checks each outcome in the next image and reports back, including when a request is out of reach or ambiguous. The tasks feature relational selection, sorting by measured properties, and environment perturbations, all simulated in Isaac Sim. No architectural change was needed. A rank-32 LoRA adapter was trained on about 40,000 samples, combining manipulation trajectories with general tool-use and pointing data, and took about six GPU-hours on a single AMD Instinct MI325X. Paired with a fine-tuned d1-2B skill monitor, we can further double recovery success under disturbances such as slips, jams and drags.

Navigation. For vision-and-language navigation, LFM3-VL-2B reads a route description and a short history of RGB frames to predict navigation targets and residual-quantized trajectory primitives, inspired by the action interface of LightNav-0. Each decision consists of five tokens: two spatial/control tokens and three hierarchically quantized codes encoding a ten-waypoint path that a velocity controller can track. We only repurpose 2,068 vocabulary tokens; the architecture is otherwise unchanged. We train on 2.8 million samples for 72 GPU-hours on MI325X GPUs. In unseen validation scenes, the resulting model achieves success rates of 53% on R2R and 43% on RxR under a strict continuous-control evaluation protocol with wall sliding disabled and explicit stopping required. We further observe robustness across varying camera angles and instruction languages. On a Jetson AGX Orin, our navigation model updates waypoint trajectories at over 2.5 Hz using TensorRT FP16 without visual prompt caching.

Manipulation. To turn LFM3-VL-2B into a vision-language-action (VLA) model, we adopt parallel action prediction inspired by OpenVLA-OFT and StarVLA-α: a small residual MLP maps the hidden states of eight action-query tokens to an eight-step chunk of continuous robot actions in a single forward pass. Proprioception is provided both as discretized text and through an embodiment-specific learned projection, and the whole network is fine-tuned end to end. We trained a single generalist checkpoint for 170 GPU-hours on MI325X GPUs, on simulated and real-robot data from 15 embodiments, ranging from single arms and mobile manipulators to bimanual platforms and a humanoid. The resulting VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks. On a Jetson AGX Orin, it can generate action chunks in under 50 ms using TensorRT at FP16 precision.

Get Started

Start building today with LFM3, available on Hugging Face and the Liquid AI API.

With LFM3, we're delivering on our vision of AI that runs anywhere. These models are:

  • Open-weight: download, fine-tune, and deploy.
  • Fast from day one: native support for llama.cpp, MLX, and vLLM across Apple, AMD, NVIDIA, SGLang and Qualcomm hardware. Deploy on Liquid Real-time Inference Pipeline for low-latency, high-volume workloads.
  • A complete family: from base models for customization to specialized text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models, one architecture covers diverse use cases.

We can't wait to see what you build.

Download on Hugging FaceUse with Liquid APITry on Playground

Launch Partners

We are grateful to our day-0 launch partners for their support. LFM3 is ready to use today across these platforms: Ambarella, AMD, Arm, Intel via OpenVINO, NVIDIA, OpenRouter, Qualcomm via Qualcomm AI Hub and GenieX, and Vercel. Thanks to Mercedes-Benz and Shopify for partnering on pre-release testing and evaluation.

Thank you to our builder ecosystem for its support: Atomic, Cactus, Hugging Face, llama.cpp, LM Studio, MLX, Ollama, RadixArk on SGLang, .txt, Unsloth, vLLM, and ZML.
